381: An army, a people, wealth, ministers, friends, a fortress — whoever holds these six is a lion among kings.
382: Fearlessness, generosity, wisdom, energy — never failing in these four is the kingly mark.
383: Vigilance, learning, bravery — a ruler of a land must never be without these three.
384: A king is one who, with manly modesty, swerves from no virtue and touches no vice.
385: A king is one who can acquire wealth, store it, guard it, and share it.
386: The world exalts the country of the ruler who is easy to approach and gentle of speech.
387: The world praises and yields to the ruler who can give kindly and protect all who come to him.
388: The ruler who does his own duty and protects his people is esteemed a god among people.
389: The world gladly shelters under a ruler who can hear bitter words without breaking.
390: He is the light of kings who holds four things: generosity, kindness, justice, and care for his people.
391: Learn thoroughly whatever you learn, and let your conduct be worthy of your learning.
393: The learned are said to have eyes. The unlearned have merely two sores in their face.
394: The learned delight all who meet them, and leave behind the wish: "When shall we meet again?"
395: The unlearned stand begging before the learned, as the destitute stand before the wealthy.
397: For the learned, every land is home and every town their own. How then can anyone die without learning?
398: What you learn in this life will please you for seven lives.
399: The learned keep longing for more, when they see learning pleases both themselves and the world.
400: Learning is the only riches that never perish. All else is not riches.
401: Speaking in a learned assembly without full knowledge is like playing chess on a board with no squares.
402: The unlearned craving to speak in council is like one who cannot bear children craving the joys of motherhood.
403: Even the unlearned are excellent, if they know how to keep silent before the learned.
404: However sharp an unlettered person's natural sense, the wise will not call it knowledge.
405: An ignoramus's pride melts the moment he speaks in a hall of the learned.
406: The unlearned are like worthless barren land: all that can be said of them is that they exist.
407: The charm of one without learning from great books is like the charm of a painted clay doll.
408: Wealth gained by the unlearned brings more sorrow than poverty brings the learned.
409: The unlearned, though born high, stand below the learned, though the learned were born low.
410: As beasts stand beside humans, so stand other people beside the learned in great works.
411: Wealth gained by the ear — learning heard — is the wealth of wealths, the chief of all wealth.
412: Learning heard is the ear's food — the truest feeding of all.
413: Whoever enjoys learning as food for the ear feasts like the gods at their offerings.
414: Even without learning, keep listening to the wise. It will be a staff in adversity.
415: The words of the good are a staff in a slippery place.
416: Listen even a little to good instruction — even that brings great dignity.
417: Those who have studied deeply and listened well will not speak foolishly, even when they have understood imperfectly.
418: The ear that instruction has never opened is deaf, though it hears.
419: Modesty and a humble mouth are rare in those never taught by the best.
420: What does it matter whether they live or die — those who judge everything by the tongue and nothing by the ear?
421: Wisdom is a weapon to ward off destruction — an inner fortress no enemy can breach.
422: Wisdom is this: not letting the mind wander where it lists, holding it from evil, and setting it on good.
423: Wisdom is to discern the truth in everything, by whomever it is spoken.
424: Wisdom is speaking so the meaning enters the hearer easily, and catching the subtlest thought hidden in others' words.
425: Wisdom wins the friendship of the great and holds it steady — not opening and closing like a lotus.
426: To live in tune with the world — that too is wisdom.
427: The wise know beforehand what will happen. Those who do not are the unwise.
428: Not fearing what ought to be feared is folly. Fearing what should be feared is the wise person's work.
429: No terrifying calamity overtakes the wise who foresee and guard against coming evils.
430: Those with wisdom possess everything. Those without it possess nothing, whatever they hold.
431: Great is the excellence of those free from pride, anger, and lust.
432: Greed, vain pride, and base pleasures are the faults of a king.
433: Those who fear guilt, if they slip as small as a millet seed, see it as large as a palmyra tree.
434: Guard against faults as against a deadly enemy — for that is exactly what they are.
435: The prosperity of one who does not guard against faults in time perishes like straw before fire.
436: What fault can remain in the ruler who has put away his own evils and watches over others'?
437: The wealth of the miser, who never spends it where he ought, wastes away and does not last.
438: Miserliness is not one fault among many. It stands alone, heavier than them all.
439: Let no one praise themselves at any time, or set their heart on useless things.
440: Whoever does not parade his desires gives his enemies nothing to work on.
441: Weigh well their worth, and win the friendship of the virtuous and the deeply learned.
442: Gather and kindly keep those who can overcome difficulties as they arise and forestall them before they come.
443: To cherish the great and win them as your own is the hardest of all hard things.
444: To win for yourself those greater than yourself — that is the highest of all powers.
445: As a ruler must use ministers as his eyes, let him examine their character well before he engages them.
446: Enemies have nothing left to do against the one who has secured the fellowship of worthy people.
447: Who could bring down a ruler served by those with the courage to rebuke him?
448: A ruler without anyone to check him perishes — even with no enemy in sight.
449: As nothing can be gained without capital, nothing lasts without worthy friends.
450: To abandon the friendship of the good is tenfold more harmful than to earn the hatred of the many.
451: True greatness fears the company of the base. Only the low-minded count them as friends.
452: As water takes the nature of the soil it flows through, so people take the character of their companions.
453: Sense is one's own; character is borrowed from one's company.
454: Wisdom seems to rest in the mind, but it really lives in a person's companions.
455: Pure company is the staff that upholds two things: purity of mind and purity of conduct.
456: The pure-hearted leave good descendants; the purely accompanied do no wrong.
457: Goodness of mind brings wealth; good society brings all praise.
458: And good companionship is strength upon strength.
459: Heaven hereafter is the fruit of a good mind — and even that ripens faster in good company.
460: No greater help than the company of the good; no greater sorrow than the company of the wicked.
461: Reflect on what will be lost, what gained, and what the final gain will be — then act.
462: Nothing is too hard for those who first think it through themselves and then weigh it fully with chosen friends.
463: The wise never chase profit by spending away their capital.
464: Those who fear reproach never begin anything they have not thought through and made clear to themselves.
465: To set out for war without weighing one's strength is one sure way to make one's enemy prosper.
466: Doing what should not be done ruins a person. So does failing to do what should be done.
467: Consider, then undertake. To say "we will consider" after undertaking is folly.
468: A task done the wrong way fails, no matter how many hands hold it up.
469: Even well-meant acts fail if done without reading the people involved.
470: Weigh your acts so they bring no reproach — the world will not support what does not befit you.
471: Weigh the strength of the deed, your own strength, the enemy's strength, and the strength of both sides' allies — then act.
472: Nothing is beyond those who, before they act, make themselves fully acquainted with their own ability and all else that is needful.
473: Many, ignorant of their own power, have marched haughtily to war and broken down in the middle of it.
474: Whoever overrates himself and acts will soon be brought down.
475: An axle will break under a cart loaded beyond its strength, even if the load were only peacocks' feathers.
476: Whoever goes out too far on a branch and ventures further will fall.
477: Know the measure of what you can give, and give within it. That is how wealth is preserved.
478: However small the income, there is no ruin while spending stays within it.
479: The prosperity of one who lives without knowing the measure of their means perishes even while it seems to continue.
480: Giving beyond one's means quickly eats up one's wealth.
481: The crow beats the owl in the day. Victory belongs to whoever picks the right time.
482: Acting at the right season is a cord that binds success unmovably.
483: What is difficult for the one who acts with the right means at the right time?
484: Even the conquest of the world can be accomplished, if one acts at the right time and the right place.
485: Those who thoughtfully wait for the right time may even conquer the world.
486: The self-restraint of the energetic while waiting is like the fighting-ram drawing back to butt.
487: The wise do not flash their anger at once. They watch their time and hold it within.
488: Respect your enemy until the fitting hour arrives; when it does, the task is easy.
489: When a rare opportunity comes, use it — while it lasts — for what cannot otherwise be done.
490: Be like the heron: still when stillness serves; strike when the moment opens.
491: Never despise an enemy or move against one, until the right ground for the attack is yours.
492: Even the strong gain much by fighting from behind strong walls.
493: Even the powerless become powerful and conquer, if they pick the right field and guard themselves well.
494: If you choose the right ground to approach your enemy, they must give up their hope of conquering you.
495: In deep water the crocodile conquers all; out of the water, other animals conquer it.
496: Chariots with mighty wheels do not run on the ocean; ocean ships do not move on land.
497: You need no other aid than fearlessness, if you think through your plan and pick the right ground.
498: A great army's strength dies on ground built for a small one.
499: It is a hazardous thing to attack people in their own country, though they lack power and fortress.
500: A fox can kill a fearless, warrior-faced elephant — if it walks into mud where its legs sink down.
501: Test a minister against four things — virtue, money, pleasure, and fear — before you choose.
502: Choose the one of good family, free from faults, with the modesty that dreads the wounds of sin.
503: Examine even the finest minds closely, and you will rarely find one without some blind spot.
504: Consider both good qualities and faults, then judge by whichever prevails.
505: Deeds are the touchstone that shows a person's greatness or littleness.
506: Do not choose the friendless and unattached. With no ties, they feel no fear of wrongdoing.
507: He who chooses without care yields all his being to folly's blind control.
508: Sorrow that will not leave even his posterity comes upon the one who chooses a stranger of unknown character.
509: Choose no one without prior consideration; once chosen, assign each their fitting duties without hesitation.
510: To choose the unexamined, and to doubt the chosen — both produce sorrow beyond remedy.
511: Employ the one whose nature leads them to choose the good, after weighing both the evil and the good in any undertaking.
512: Give the work to the one who can enlarge revenue, increase wealth, and thoughtfully prevent accidents that would destroy it.
513: Let the choice fall on the one richly endowed with four things: love, knowledge, a clear mind, and freedom from greed.
514: However thoroughly you test people, some change with the work you give them.
515: A ruler's work is done only by the wise and patient — never assign it out of mere personal attachment.
516: Act after considering the agent, the deed, and the time suitable to it.
517: Having considered "this person can do this, by these means," leave the task with them.
518: Having weighed what work a person is fit for, employ them in that.
519: Prosperity walks away from the ruler who doubts a loyal servant.
520: Check your servants' conduct daily. If they keep straight, the world will keep straight too.
